Air Force Pumps $3.5M in Blended-Wing-Body Cargo Drone Made by Natilus
20 photos
Photo: Natilus
For several years now, an American aerospace company called Natilus has been trying to come up with a new way of designing aircraft. Ok, not entirely new, but never attempted on such a scale before. And that new way of designing an aircraft, blended-wing-body (BWB), just got a major boost thanks to official military backing.
The Natilus product the Air Force sees as potentially useful for its needs is called Kona, and it is a BWB in that it comes with no clear distinction between its main fuselage and its wings. By trade, it is an optionally piloted aircraft born to carry cargo.
The company chose to go down the path of a BWB design on account of the advantages it brings along compared to a conventional setup. That includes, among other things, more lifting power, less drag, and more interior space.
In the case of the Kona, as in the specific design being researched right now for the needs of the USAF, that translates into a 3.8-ton lifting capability and a maximum range of 920 miles (1,481 km).
These capabilities place the mildly strange-looking aircraft smack down between what a light utility aircraft the likes of the Cessna C-208 and a heavy-lift Lockheed C-130 Hercules can do. Moreover, the Kona also throws in the ability to take off and land from and on short fields and without a pilot on board.
On top of everything, it has been imagined in such a way as to be compatible with existing cargo infrastructure, and its fuel consumption needs should be some 30 percent lower than in the case of conventional aircraft of similar size.
I said earlier that the U.S. military is very interested in this design, and one only needs to look at the $3.5 million it pumped at the beginning of the month into research, development, test, and evaluation of the Kona .
The company plans to use the money to speed up work, aiming for full-scale flight testing and an operationally relevant U.S. Joint Force demonstration at a yet-undisclosed time in the future.
Initially, the company started work on the BWB with the civilian sector in mind, but, as with many other aerospace innovations, it has immediately attracted the eye of the military. That's because, aside from being able to carry cargo, it could be adapted to perform communications relay missions and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) flights.
There is no word yet on when the militarized Kona will be ready, but the company did reveal that it is now moving to Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Part 23 certification (normal category airplanes up to 19 seats) and full-scale flight testing. We'll keep an eye on things and report back when that (or some other) milestone is reached.
